title: Tiny-request pacing bakeoff — lab notes (personal)
content:
Purpose:
Quick informal bakeoff comparing simple dispatch strategies for tiny requests (<= 8 tokens / single-turn completions). Goal: quantify tradeoffs between immediate dispatch, fixed micro-window batching, and an adaptive pacing heuristic that uses backlog smoothing + max-wait cap. Personal notes — not polished.

Background / why I care:
- Tiny requests are common in product features (autocomplete, short assistant pings, slot filling).
- Serving runtime is optimized for larger slices; tiny requests can kill throughput (high overhead per request) or hurt tail if we wait too long to batch.
- Want a practical default heuristic that improves unit cost and throughput without blowing p99 for interactive flows.

Environment:
- Cluster: 1x A100 (40GB) dev rig, locally isolated workload.
- Runtime: redwood-serving-edge v1.8.2 (local build).
- Model: open-llama-7b-quant-v2 (int8-like profile).
- Client: loadgen v0.7.0, Poisson arrival with controlled mean QPS.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 (ms), throughput (req/s), batch-size distribution, GPU util %.

Method:
- Three strategies:
  1) immediate: dispatch as soon as request arrives (no batching).
  2) fixed-window-4ms: hold incoming requests up to 4ms or until GPU ready; then dispatch batch.
  3) adaptive-pacer: dynamic hold based on recent backlog rate with cap 8ms and min immediate if backlog=0. smoothing alpha=0.2.
- Workload: 1) steady 4k rps (tiny requests), 2) ramp 1k->12k rps over 3 minutes, 3) spike test: 10s surge to 20k rps every 2 minutes.
- Each run: 3x 5min trials, warmup 60s.

Commands I ran (notes):
- loadgen command: ./loadgen --qps 4000 --tokens 6 --dist poisson --clients 64 --duration 300 --trace p95
- runtime flags toggled: --batch-window-ms=0/4/8 and --adaptive-pacer=on/off.

Representative aggregated results (steady 4k rps):
- immediate: p50 12ms, p95 34ms, p99 80ms, throughput 3950 rps, avg batch size ~1.2, GPU util 18%
- fixed-window-4ms: p50 14ms, p95 23ms, p99 50ms, throughput 8200 rps, avg batch size ~3.6, GPU util 46%
- adaptive-pacer (cap 8ms): p50 16ms, p95 20ms, p99 36ms, throughput 11,900 rps, avg batch size ~5.1, GPU util 68%

Notes on spike test (10s surge to 20k rps):
- immediate: p99 rockets to 450ms during surge; many requests starved the GPU pipeline (no batching).
- fixed-window-4ms: p99 ~220ms, but observed queue buildup after surge; recovery ~25s to steady throughput.
- adaptive-pacer: p99 ~130ms peak, backlog smoothing prevented aggressive queuing, recovery ~8s.

Quick ascii visualization (p95 ms across configs, steady 4k):
- immediate  : ################## 34ms
- window-4ms : ########### 23ms
- adaptive   : ######## 20ms

Observations / hypotheses:
- Short fixed windows (4ms) are a big win vs immediate dispatch: ~2x throughput in this env, better p95.
- Adaptive pacing with a modest cap produces the best throughput while keeping tail relatively controlled; it benefits from higher average batch sizes but avoids long tails during spikes by reducing hold when backlog drops.
- GPU utilization correlates strongly with avg batch size and explains throughput differences. Tiny requests waste a lot of GPU cycles when dispatched singly.
- p99 improvements are real but sensitive to the cap; too-large caps (>=16ms) make p99 worse under sudden low-latency demands.

Practical takeaway for defaults (opinionated):
- Enable an adaptive paced batching by default on tiny-request endpoints with: min-hold 0ms, smoothing alpha 0.15, max-cap 6-8ms.
- Provide per-route override for latency-sensitive interactive flows to force immediate or smaller caps.

Telemetry gotchas I noticed:
- p99 sampling granularity matters; using 1s buckets smoothed peaks too much. Use 100ms buckets for spike tests.
- Client-side queue times (network + agent) must be subtracted when measuring pure RPC/serving latency — I saw +5–8ms variance there.

Next steps / experiments to run:
- Run same bakeoff on mixed-request size workload (10% large requests) to see interference.
- Try different smoothing alphas and caps systematically (grid search).
- Validate on multi-GPU stacked inference path (synchronous model shard) — check scheduling overhead.
- Cost calc: roughly estimate token-cost reduction if we can run 2x requests per GPU-second on prod tier.

Open questions / unresolved:
- How does adaptive pacing interact with prefix/KV-cache warmup for multi-turn flows? Could longer holds reduce cache reuse?
- Are there fairness issues across tenants if one tenant's tiny requests are batched aggressively? Need tenant-aware caps.

Notes-to-self:
- Save loadgen scripts to bench repo (PR referenced above).
- If adopting adaptive default, add rollout flags and canary to 5% of traffic.
- Bring results to eng-serving-runtime sync next Wed — present quick slides (2–3).

End of scratchpad.
